source.title: Learning Gaussian Multi-Index Models with Gradient Flow: Time Complexity and Directional Convergence
source.authors: Berfin Şimşek; Amire Bendjeddou; Daniel Hsu

record.tranche_reason: Reports gradient-flow convergence and failure in Gaussian multi-index teacher-student models, a different setting from the classification-error versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports population correlation-loss gradient flow on Gaussian data, including theoretical convergence results and simulations. Those results concern index-vector recovery and directional convergence, not training classification error on CIFAR or the specific conditions in V1–V6. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study cites V2's original ReLU result but studies directional recovery under population correlation loss with different activations. It does not measure spurious-minimum frequencies in the stated ReLU setting or the effect of adding one or two neurons. Its results do not test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the main conclusion: orthogonal directions admit nearest-direction convergence under the stated assumptions, logarithmic-factor width enables direction coverage, and sufficiently close equiangular directions can attract flow toward an average instead. Qualify the random-initialization guarantee by the proof's positivity assumptions or even-activation extension. The displayed union bound gives k^(-ϵ), not universally 1/k. Provable MSE improvements remain open.
record.recipe_differences: Population gradient flow on a stylized Gaussian multi-index teacher-student model with correlation loss and unit-norm neurons; the reported simulations also compare MSE loss. It does not use the benchmark classification recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Index-vector geometry and dot product β change the directional outcome; initialization correlations determine the nearest direction; target activation and information exponent affect time complexity and convergence conditions; correlation loss versus MSE changes neuron allocation behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: For orthogonal index vectors, the largest initial positive correlation determines the limiting direction; tied maxima yield a normalized average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated activation and initialization assumptions, population correlation-loss flow selects the nearest orthogonal index direction.

fits_no_version.finding: The coupon-collection calculation gives failure probability at most k^(-ϵ) with (1+ϵ)k ln k neurons, while proportional width has a nonvanishing asymptotic lower bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Logarithmic-factor width improves initialization coverage of orthogonal index directions under decoupled correlation-loss dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: The average-direction fixed point becomes a local minimum for sufficiently close equiangular directions; simulations show convergence to that average above an attraction threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Index-vector geometry can prevent individual-direction recovery under population correlation-loss flow.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed unlucky initialization, MSE recovers a direction missed by correlation loss. Simulations also suggest faster dynamics with MSE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interactions between student neurons under MSE can improve directional allocation relative to decoupled correlation loss.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2025; PMLR Volume 258)
record.problems: The model is stylized: population loss, standard Gaussian inputs, unit-norm neurons, and a sum of single-index teachers. The authors note that they use correlation loss instead of MSE for the main analysis and that MSE interactions complicate analysis. Numerical results are described qualitatively in figure captions and text; no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows were left out. Figure-only curve values were not reconstructed; the text describes qualitative Figure 4 behavior, recorded in R9 and R10.

untested.parts: Convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR, including random or corrupted labels, under SGD or Adam.
Spurious-minimum convergence frequencies in two-layer ReLU teacher-student models as widths grow together, and the benefit of one or two extra student neurons.
Depth-related training degradation and comparisons involving identity shortcuts, special initialization, or normalization.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation through depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth.
Finite learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature evolution, recovery, and divergence.
Batch normalization's training-speed and learning-rate benefits, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6 because their measures fit no version; this does not dispute the reported directional phenomena. No omitted result bears directly on a stated version.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR classification error, random or corrupted labels, SGD or Adam, model size and training duration.
The stated ReLU teacher-student setting, the frequency of spurious local minima as teacher and student grow together, and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Depth, batch normalization, identity shortcuts, and the stated deep-network training comparisons.
Comparisons of initialization schemes, activation-matched initialization, and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to a stability threshold, loss and curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons of training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: single neuron
rows.operation_detail: Correlation-loss gradient flow with orthogonal index vectors; nearest-index directional convergence is characterized theoretically.

conditions.value: positive dot products; a unique maximum, or tied maxima
σ* = h_p* with p* ≥ 3; Proposition 2.2 also permits the stated broader activation conditions

rows.value: The neuron converges to the nearest index vector; tied maxima lead to the normalized average of the tied vectors.
rows.note: This is a directional-convergence result, not a classification-error measure.
rows.check: Directional convergence does not measure any stated version. The result requires positive initial correlations, with a sign-adjusted extension for even activations.

rows.subject: n student neurons
rows.operation_detail: Correlation-loss gradient flow with orthogonal index vectors and random neuron initialization; a coupon-collecting bound gives a high-probability condition for collecting every index direction.

conditions.value: neurons sampled independently and uniformly on the sphere

rows.measure: probability that some index vector is not collected by any neuron at initialization
rows.note: The bound concerns initialization allocation and the resulting directional convergence, not training classification error.
rows.check: Initialization coverage is outside the versions. Equation (5) gives failure probability at most k^(-ϵ) for n ≥ (1+ϵ)k ln k, not below 1/k for every ϵ > 0. Also, applying directional convergence to unrestricted sphere initialization needs qualification: the proof assumes positive initial correlations except for even activations.

rows.subject: n student neurons
rows.operation_detail: Correlation-loss gradient flow with orthogonal index vectors; a lower bound is given for failing to allocate a neuron to every direction.
rows.measure: probability that some index vector is not collected by any neuron at initialization
rows.value: failure probability is more than exp(−γ) in the proportional limit
rows.note: The paper says constant-factor overparameterization does not guarantee matching all directions under correlation loss.
rows.check: Coverage failure is outside the versions. Equation (6) gives a lower bound tending to exp(−γ); describe this as an asymptotic lower bound, rather than a strict finite-k bound above exp(−γ).

rows.subject: single neuron
rows.operation_detail: Correlation-loss gradient flow with equiangular index vectors; the curvature of the average-direction fixed point is analyzed theoretically.

conditions.value: polynomial of degree P and information exponent p*

rows.measure: local geometry of the average-direction fixed point
rows.value: The average-direction fixed point is a strict saddle.
rows.note: This characterizes a fixed point, not classification error.
rows.check: Local geometry for a single neuron with polynomial target activation does not test V2's ReLU width comparison or any other version.

rows.subject: single neuron
rows.operation_detail: Correlation-loss gradient flow with equiangular index vectors; the curvature of the average-direction fixed point is analyzed theoretically.

conditions.value: polynomial of degree P and information exponent p*

rows.measure: local geometry of the average-direction fixed point
rows.value: The average-direction fixed point is a local minimum.
rows.note: The theorem gives a saddle condition and a local-minimum condition; these do not cover the gap between their thresholds for general polynomial targets.
rows.check: The average-direction local minimum is outside the stated versions; its existence alone does not establish V2's frequency of convergence to spurious minima.

rows.subject: single neuron
rows.operation_detail: Correlation-loss gradient descent on the sphere with equiangular index vectors; the reported bifurcation changes the limiting direction.
rows.value: At a critical β_f ∈ (0, 1), behavior changes from monotonic convergence to the nearest direction to non-monotonic convergence to the average of directions.
rows.note: The caption describes the qualitative simulation result; it does not give a numerical value for β_f.
rows.check: The geometry-dependent directional transition is outside the versions. The simulated attraction threshold β_f must remain distinct from the theoretical curvature threshold β_c.

rows.subject: n = 10 student neurons
rows.operation_detail: Compared correlation loss with MSE loss for orthogonal index vectors and an initialization with no neuron closest to one index vector.

conditions.value: fixed; no neuron initially closest to one index vector

rows.measure: whether gradient flow finds every index direction
rows.baseline: MSE loss: the paper states that repulsion between neurons fixes the issue
rows.value: Gradient flow fails to find the missing index direction.
rows.note: This is a toy directional-recovery comparison; the caption gives no numerical error values.
rows.check: Missing an index direction under correlation loss does not measure a stated version. Figure 3 states k=2 and n=10 but does not explicitly state d=1000 in the supplied text.

rows.subject: n = 10 student neurons
rows.operation_detail: Compared MSE loss with correlation loss for orthogonal index vectors and an initialization with no neuron closest to one index vector.

conditions.value: fixed; no neuron initially closest to one index vector

rows.measure: whether gradient flow finds every index direction
rows.baseline: Correlation loss: gradient flow fails to find the missing index direction
rows.value: MSE loss fixes this issue thanks to repulsion between neurons.
rows.note: This comparison concerns recovery of index directions, not classification error.
rows.check: The MSE allocation improvement does not measure a stated version. Figure 3 does not explicitly state d=1000 in the supplied text.

rows.subject: n = 10 student neurons
rows.operation_detail: Compared MSE loss with correlation loss for orthogonal index vectors and odd or even target activations.
rows.measure: training dynamics, trajectories, and loss curves
rows.baseline: correlation loss: the comparison reference; figure gives loss curves
rows.value: MSE behaves similarly to correlation loss early in training when there is no linear or quadratic component; adding the MSE repulsion term virtually decreases time complexity, with improvement possibly only up to a constant factor.
rows.note: The paper describes qualitative behavior and does not provide numerical values for the curves.
rows.check: A loss-function comparison does not test initialization, normalization, or learning-rate stability. The possible constant-factor speed improvement is a qualitative observation, not an established complexity bound.

rows.subject: n = 10 student neurons
rows.operation_detail: Compared MSE loss with correlation loss for orthogonal index vectors and odd or even target activations.
rows.measure: training dynamics, trajectories, and loss curves
rows.baseline: correlation loss: the comparison reference; figure gives loss curves
rows.value: The winning neurons move toward the closest index vectors under MSE loss; other neurons move non-trivially due to interactions. Adding the MSE repulsion term virtually decreases time complexity, with improvement possibly only up to a constant factor.
rows.note: The paper describes qualitative behavior and does not provide numerical values for the curves.
rows.check: A loss-function comparison does not measure any stated version. The possible constant-factor speed improvement is a qualitative observation, not an established complexity bound.
